name: plf::bitset (plf_bitsets)
workload: Full bitset test-suite exercised in a loop (set/reset/shift/index/etc.); separately, set_range/reset_range on a 128000-bit bitset over 10000 randomly chosen ranges per run.
claimed_speedup: Release (O2, AVX2): 24% (GCC)/20% (MSVC) faster overall test suite; 34,652%/67,612% faster set_range/reset_range; ~101%/98% faster left/right shift (GCC), 35%/22% (MSVC); 6%/204% faster set(pos,val); 3%/0% faster operator[]. Debug builds show much larger gaps (up to 428,127%/750,726% for set_range/reset_range).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2 (nuwen mingw) and MSVC 2022; release build: O2, AVX2, C++23
tradeoffs: plf::bitset omits std::bitset's from-string/from-ulong constructors; adds set_range/reset_range, range-based any/all/none/count, an allocation-free XOR swap, index-bounds-checking via a template flag, and a user-supplied-buffer variant (plf::bitsetb) not present in std::bitset.
caveats: First-party benchmark (project author's own numbers), not independently reproduced, though methodology (compiler, flags, hardware) and full benchmark source are published. The extreme set_range/reset_range percentages (up to ~677x) largely reflect that std::bitset has no native ranged-set primitive (callers must loop bit-by-bit), so this is partly an algorithmic-complexity win (O(1) words vs O(n) bits) rather than a raw constant-factor speedup; the overall test-suite numbers (~20-24%) are the more representative figure for general use. Licensed under 'Computing For Good License v1.01' (zlib-like but with additional ethical-use-restriction clauses 4a-4e), which is not OSI-approved due to those field-of-use restrictions, so usability is 'reference' rather than 'copyable'.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'bitset faster than std::bitset benchmark github' -> https://github.com/mattreecebentley/plf_bitsets; full methodology at https://plflib.org/bitsets.htm

name: better_bitset
workload: Find index of first set bit ('first_one') across bitsets of size 4-8192 bits, ~5 average one-bits per bitset, 1000 random bitsets per size, measured with Google Benchmark; the std::bitset side is a manual bit-by-bit loop using .test(i), since std::bitset has no built-in bit-scan for sizes above 64.
claimed_speedup: README claims 'improvements averaging 60x' versus the iterative std::bitset approach. benchmark/results.txt shows e.g. N=8192: 953,294 ns (std::bitset loop) vs 18,134 ns (better_bitset) = ~52.6x faster (derived from page data); N=64: 6,349 ns vs 213 ns = ~29.8x faster (derived from page data); N=8: 701 ns vs 218 ns = ~3.2x faster (derived from page data).
hardware: 20 logical CPUs @ ~3609.6 MHz (Google Benchmark auto-detected clock speed and cache sizes only; exact CPU model name not recorded)
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement: only implements first_zero/first_one plus the common subset (all/any/none/count/size/set/reset/flip/to_string); lacks bitwise operators and the std::bitset reference-proxy type. Also smaller than std::bitset for sizes <=16 bits.
caveats: Small, unmaintained (last commit 2022, 8 stars) repo. Benchmark is first-party and its results.txt (Google Benchmark output) records no compiler name or optimization flags, and identifies the CPU only by core count/clock speed rather than model, so it falls short of Tier A methodology despite having public benchmark code and real numbers. No LICENSE file in the repo, so the code can be studied but not safely reused.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch '"Bitset2" ClaasBontus header-only bitset benchmark std::bitset' surfaced https://github.com/MrElectrify/better_bitset; benchmark folder and results opened at github.com/MrElectrify/better_bitset/tree/master/benchmark

name: CRoaring (Roaring Bitmaps)
baseline: uncompressed bitset with the same word-array representation as std::bitset/std::vector<bool> (the paper's own portable C reimplementation, 'cbitset', is used in the benchmark rather than literally std::bitset or std::vector<bool>)
workload: 8 realistic integer-set datasets (CensusInc, CensusInc-sorted, Census1881, Census1881-sorted, Weather, Weather-sorted, Wikileaks, Wikileaks-sorted; 200 sets each, universe sizes 200K-4.3M): sequential iteration/cardinality, random-access membership queries at n/4, n/2, 3n/4, and 199 pairwise intersections/unions/differences/symmetric differences between successive sets. Reported as CPU cycles per input value.
claimed_speedup: Mixed by dataset and operation. Intersections (Table 7a, cycles/value): bitset 19.5 vs Roaring 0.090 on Census1881 (~217x faster, derived from page data); bitset 33.0 vs Roaring 0.140 on Census1881-sorted (~236x, derived from page data); bitset 26.4 vs Roaring 1.43 on Wikileaks (~18x, derived from page data). But on CensusInc/CensusInc-sorted/Weather, the plain bitset is FASTER than Roaring (e.g. bitset 0.130 vs Roaring 0.220-0.380 cycles/value on CensusInc, i.e. bitset ~1.7-2.9x faster there). Random-access membership queries (Table 6): plain bitset wins on every dataset (2.4-3.7 cycles vs Roaring's 17-77 cycles). Memory (Table 4): Roaring uses far less than an uncompressed bitset on sparse data, e.g. 2.60 vs 524 bits/value on Census1881, 0.34 vs 11.4 bits/value on Weather-sorted.
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (Skylake, 3.4 GHz, 32KB L1d, 256KB L2/core, 8MB L3), 32GB DDR4-2133 dual-channel, single-threaded, Turbo Boost disabled, timed with rdtsc, results reproducible within 5%
stars_or_usage: 1,887 stars; used by Apache Doris, ClickHouse, Alibaba Tair, Redpanda, YDB, StarRocks
tradeoffs: Roaring wins decisively on memory and on set-algebra over sparse/clustered 32-bit integer sets, but loses to a plain uncompressed bitset on random-access membership queries (bitset has roughly an order of magnitude lower latency) and can lose on set-algebra for dense/small-universe datasets. Targets dynamic sparse 32-bit integer sets, not fixed-size dense bit flags, so it is not a general drop-in for std::bitset<N> or std::vector<bool>.
caveats: The paper's 'bitset' baseline is the authors' own portable C library ('cbitset', github.com/lemire/cbitset: ceil(n/64) 64-bit words, no processor-specific optimizations), not literally std::bitset or std::vector<bool> from a standard library implementation, though it is representationally identical to both, so baseline_in_list is recorded true with reduced confidence. Results are strongly dataset- and operation-dependent; the entry reports both wins and losses rather than a single headline number. Authors of the paper are also the library's maintainers (Lemire et al., published in Software: Practice and Experience, 2018), but code, compiler, flags, and CPU model are all public and stated, satisfying Tier A methodology regardless of who ran it.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'CRoaring roaring bitmap benchmark std::bitset std::vector<bool>' -> https://github.com/RoaringBitmap/CRoaring; benchmark tables opened via https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.07821 (Lemire, Kaser, Kurz, Deri, O'Hara, Saint-Jacques, Ssi-Yan-Kai)

name: sdsl::bit_vector (SDSL - Succinct Data Structure Library)
claimed_speedup: Project's own description (SDSL 3.0 docs/wiki): sdsl::bit_vector is 'an optimized replacement of the infamous std::vector<bool>'. No numeric benchmark located for this specific claim within the research budget.
stars_or_usage: 2,309 stars; de facto standard succinct-data-structures library, extremely widely cited in the IR/bioinformatics/text-indexing literature (e.g. underlies the SPIRE 2014 sdsl-lite paper and dozens of downstream tools)
tradeoffs: bit_vector itself is a packed bit array similar in spirit to std::vector<bool> but without a standard-library iterator/allocator interface or thread-safety guarantees for concurrent bit writes; the library's real value is the rank/select/compressed layers built on top (rrr_vector, sd_vector, wt_*), which are not literal std::vector<bool>/std::bitset drop-ins and add their own space/time tradeoffs.
caveats: Could not confirm a specific numeric benchmark for bit_vector vs std::vector<bool> within the tool budget for this run; the 'optimized replacement' framing is a first-party claim with no accompanying numbers found, so this is Tier D. Included as this run's one allowed Tier-D entry because the project is unambiguously notable (2.3k stars, foundational in its field). Repository has not been pushed to since 2023-06-02 (>3 years), so maintenance_status is 'abandoned' despite the project's continued heavy citation/usage.
